analysis.one_liner: Lets the Postal Service offer banking, broadband, alcohol shipping, and other new services to raise revenue.
analysis.headline: The Postal Innovation Act was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee in July 2015 and never received a vote or any further action before Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the U.S. Postal Service offer nonpostal services—like basic financial services, warehousing, public internet access, and shipping beer, wine, and spirits—using its existing stores, trucks, and workers to bring in new revenue. It would also let the Postal Service provide services to state, local, and tribal governments, run pilot programs in five cities testing broadband and other offerings, upgrade its aging vehicle fleet with cleaner, safer vehicles, and require a government study on postal broadband and internet voting.
analysis.who_benefits: Postal customers and communities—especially rural areas and postal deserts where banks are scarce—gain access to basic financial services like check cashing and small-dollar products at post offices, plus potentially cheaper broadband and alcohol shipping options. The Postal Service itself gains new revenue streams to shore up its finances, protecting delivery jobs and universal service, and its workers benefit from a safer, more fuel-efficient vehicle fleet.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Postal customers, rural communities, and USPS workers

how_it_helps.text: Amends postal law to let the Postal Service provide nonpostal services including financial services, warehousing, public internet access, and shipment of beer, wine, and spirits, provided they use the Postal Service's existing network and improve its finances [S2][S3].
Authorizes the Postal Service to furnish property and services to state, local, and tribal governments, opening partnerships for services like passport acceptance at the local level [S2][S3].

Creates a pilot program in five cities—including at least one rural and one urban post office—to test how cost-effectively nonpostal services like municipal broadband, emergency broadband, financial services, and internet voting can be delivered through public-private partnerships [S2][S3].

Lets the Postal Service contract to upgrade its vehicle fleet to cut collision, maintenance, and fuel costs, and requires fuel-economy guidelines, crash-avoidance safety technology, and at least a 2% annual reduction in petroleum use through fiscal year 2025 [S2][S3].
Requires a Government Accountability Office study on the opportunities and challenges of Postal Service-provided public broadband internet and internet voting [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Any costs of setting up new nonpostal services would be borne by the Postal Service, offset by the requirement that new services use its existing network and have the potential to improve its financial position. Commercial banks, broadband providers, and shipping companies could lose some business if the Postal Service competes in financial services, internet access, and alcohol shipping, though those costs depend on how far the new services actually scaled. Taxpayers face no direct new appropriation in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private banks, broadband providers, and shipping carriers

drawbacks.text: The bill directs the Postal Service into commercial markets—banking, broadband, alcohol shipping—where private firms already operate, and critics of such proposals argue the agency lacks the regulatory expertise and capital to compete safely in financial services without exposing itself to new liabilities [S3].

The pilot program relies on public-private partnerships whose terms, costs, and revenue-sharing are left to the Postal Service to determine, giving the agency wide discretion without detailed guardrails in the bill text [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and wide-reaching: new revenue for a self-funding agency, expanded access to basic financial services in underbanked areas, safer and cleaner vehicles, and better data (via the GAO study) on postal broadband and voting. The main risks are execution risk—launching commercial services in competitive markets with limited expertise—and the possibility that public-private partnerships could favor private intermediaries over direct public provision. On balance, the bill's safeguards (requiring use of existing USPS infrastructure and net financial improvement) keep the downside modest.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to committee in the Senate, the bill sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the 114th Congress and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced S. 1854, the Postal Innovation Act, on July 23, 2015 [S1][S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs on July 23, 2015 [S5].
No further action was taken—the bill never received a hearing, committee markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Postal Service's would-be private competitors in financial services, broadband, and package delivery benefited, since postal expansion never materialized. Communities without bank access and the Postal Service itself lost the potential new revenue and services the bill would have tested.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: USPS's private-sector competitors in banking and broadband

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Postal Innovation Act to let the Postal Service offer financial services, broadband, and other nonpostal services and to upgrade its vehicle fleet [S1][S2][S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors and no recorded floor opposition—no votes were ever taken—so the partisan alignment on the bill cannot be determined from the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would let USPS use its existing retail, delivery, and transport network to offer new revenue-generating services, improving its finances without cutting service or jobs. A stronger Postal Service supports universal, affordable delivery for the public.

Postal financial services would compete with banks and high-fee check-cashing and small-dollar lenders, particularly in underserved areas where those businesses charge the highest fees. Their loss of a captive market would be a direct gain for postal customers.

Public and municipal broadband pilots through post offices could compete with commercial internet providers in some markets, but the bill also envisions public-private partnerships that could channel contracts to those same providers.

Allowing USPS to ship beer, wine, and spirits would take business from private carriers that currently handle legal alcohol shipping, potentially lowering shipping costs for consumers and small wineries and breweries.

industries.industry: Vehicle manufacturers and fleet technology suppliers
industries.note: Fleet upgrade contracts for fuel-efficient, crash-avoidance-equipped vehicles would create demand for automakers and safety-technology suppliers, while giving postal carriers safer, cleaner trucks.
